dm: Chapter Eight: The Exposition of Meditative Concentration
gm: Chapter Eight: Teaching Meditation

dm: Having thus generated diligence, One should place the mind in meditative concentration. A person whose mind is distracted Dwells between the fangs of the mental afflictions.
gm: Having thus generated joyous effort, One should place the mind in meditative concentration. A person whose mind is distracted Dwells between the fangs of the afflictions.

dm: Through solitude of body and mind, Distractions will not arise. Therefore, one should renounce the world And completely cast aside discursive thoughts.
gm: Through the isolation of body and mind, Distraction does not arise. Therefore, one should abandon the worldly life And completely discard discursive thoughts.

dm: Because of attachment and craving for gain and the like, One does not renounce the world. Therefore, completely abandon these things, And the wise should analyze in this way.
gm: Because of attachment and for the sake of gain and so forth, Through craving, one does not abandon the world. Therefore, having completely abandoned these, The wise should analyze in this way.

dm: Through special insight thoroughly conjoined with calm abiding, One should understand that the mental afflictions are completely destroyed. Therefore, one should first seek calm abiding; This is achieved by those who find genuine delight in detachment from the world.
gm: By special insight completely endowed with calm abiding, Knowing that the afflictions are destroyed, One should first seek calm abiding; and that too Is accomplished by joyful detachment from the world.

dm: Since all is impermanent, who that is impermanent Would feel a true attachment to another? Because of that, for thousands of lifetimes, One will never again see the beloved.
gm: What impermanent being Would be truly attached to the impermanent? Through that, for thousands of lifetimes, They will not see their loved ones.

dm: If they are not seen, there is no joy, And the mind will not remain in meditative equipoise; Even if they are seen, there is no satisfaction, And one is tormented by craving just as before.
gm: Not seeing them, one will not be joyful, And the mind will not rest in equipoise. Even seeing them, one will not be satisfied, And will be tormented by craving as before.

dm: If one is attached to sentient beings, The perfect reality is completely obscured. It destroys even a mind of disillusionment, And in the end, one will be tormented by grief.
gm: If one forms attachments to sentient beings, Ultimate reality is completely obscured, The mind of disillusionment is also destroyed, And in the end, one will be tormented by sorrow.

dm: By thinking only of them, This life will pass away in vain. Through impermanent friendships, Even the eternal Dharma is destroyed.
gm: By merely thinking about them, This life will pass away meaninglessly. Because of impermanent friends and relatives, Even the eternal Dharma will be destroyed.

dm: If one shares the same conduct as the foolish, One will certainly go to the lower realms. If they lead one to what is unwholesome, What is the use of relying on the childish?
gm: If one acts with equal fortune to the childish, One will certainly go to the lower realms. If they lead one to what is unequal, What is the use of relying on the childish?

dm: In a single instant they become friends, And in a mere moment they turn into enemies. Because they react with anger toward things that should bring joy, Ordinary beings are difficult to please.
gm: In a single instant they become friends, And in a brief moment they even become enemies. Since they become angry at causes for joy, Ordinary people are difficult to please.

dm: If one speaks for their benefit, they become angry, And they even turn one away from what is helpful. If their own words are not heeded, They become enraged and will fall into the lower realms.
gm: If one speaks beneficially, they get angry, And they turn me away from what is beneficial. If one does not listen to their words, They become angry and go to the lower realms.

dm: They are jealous of superiors and competitive with equals; They are arrogant toward inferiors and conceited when praised. If something unpleasant is said, they become angry; When could one ever receive benefit from a fool?
gm: Envious of superiors, competitive with equals, Arrogant toward inferiors, conceited when praised, And prone to anger when spoken to unpleasantly— When is benefit ever obtained from the childish?

dm: If one associates with the childish, then from such childishness, Self-praise, the disparagement of others, And talk that delights in cyclic existence and the like, All manner of non-virtue will certainly arise.
gm: If one associates with the childish, Praising oneself and disparaging others, And talking about the joys of cyclic existence and so forth, Non-virtue will certainly arise in every way.

dm: Thus, relying on one another in such a way Will result in nothing but ruin; Since they do not accomplish my purpose, And I will not be of benefit to them either.
gm: Thus, associating oneself with others Will merely lead to ruin. They will not accomplish my benefit, And I will not accomplish their benefit.

dm: I shall flee far away from the childish. If I encounter them, I shall please them with a joyful manner, Yet without becoming overly intimate, I shall maintain a polite and ordinary relationship.
gm: One should flee far away from the childish. When meeting them, one should please them with joy, Without becoming very close, Interacting well as mere acquaintances.

dm: Like a bee taking nectar from a flower, Take only that which is meaningful for the Dharma; And remain without intimacy toward anyone, As if you had never seen them before.
gm: Like a bee taking nectar from a flower, Having taken only the meaning of Dharma, As if never having seen them before, One should remain without familiarity toward everyone.

dm: If I harbor such pride, thinking, "I have many gains and honors, And many people are fond of me," Then fear will arise after death.
gm: "I have much gain and respect," "Many are fond of me"— If one harbors such conceit, Fear will arise after death.

dm: Therefore, whatever it is that your deluded mind Becomes attached to, Those very things will combine to arise As suffering, multiplied a thousandfold.
gm: Therefore, whatever the thoroughly deluded mind Becomes attached to, Along with that, a thousandfold Suffering will manifest and arise.

dm: Therefore, the wise should not form attachments, For from attachment, fear is born. Since these things are by nature subject to loss, Remain steadfast and understand this well.
gm: Therefore, the wise should not be attached; From attachment, fear arises. Since these will naturally be left behind, Remain steadfast and fully understand this.

dm: Though one may acquire many gains, And though fame and renown may arise, Even with a collection of gain and fame, There is no knowing where one will go.
gm: Even if many gains are acquired, And fame and a good reputation arise, Together with the collection of gains and fame, There is no knowing where one will go.

dm: If there are others who disparage me, What reason is there for me to be pleased by praise? If there are others who praise me, What reason is there for me to be displeased by disparagement?
gm: If there are others who disparage me, What joy is there for me in praise? If there are others who praise me, What displeasure is there in disparagement?

dm: Since sentient beings have such diverse inclinations, Even the Victors cannot satisfy them all; What need is there to mention a wretched person like me? Therefore, I shall abandon concern for the world's opinions.
gm: Sentient beings have diverse inclinations; If even the Victors cannot please them, What need to mention an inferior one like me? Therefore, I should abandon worldly thoughts.

dm: Sentient beings disparage those who have no possessions, And speak ill of those who have them. Since they are by nature so difficult to get along with, How can any joy arise from associating with them?
gm: Sentient beings disparage those without gains, And speak unpleasantly of those with gains. With those who are naturally difficult to associate with, How can joy ever arise?

dm: Because the childish find no pleasure Unless their own interests are served, The Tathāgatas have said that no childish person is a friend; Thus have the Tathāgatas spoken.
gm: Because the childish do not experience joy Unless it is for their own benefit, "None of the childish are true friends," Thus the Tathāgatas have spoken.

dm: In the forest, the wild animals, the birds, and the trees Do not speak unpleasant words. When shall I come to dwell together With those whose company is a delight?
gm: In the forest, deer and birds, And trees do not speak unpleasantly; With those whose company is joyful, When will I dwell together?

dm: Having made my home in a cave, an empty temple, or at the foot of a tree, When shall I come to be without attachment, Never looking back, And become free from all clinging?
gm: In a cave or an empty shrine, Or dwelling at the foot of a tree, When will I never look back, And become free from attachment?

dm: When shall I dwell in vast, naturally spacious regions That are not claimed as "mine," Acting with total freedom And without attachment?
gm: In places not held as "mine", Which are naturally vast, Acting freely and without attachment, When will I abide?

dm: Possessing only a few items such as an alms bowl, And wearing clothes that no one else desires, When shall I come to dwell without fear, Even without attempting to conceal this body?
gm: With merely a begging bowl and the like, Wearing garments unwanted by anyone, And not even concealing this body, When will I dwell fearlessly?

dm: Having gone to a charnel ground, When shall I come to treat as equal My own body and the skeletal remains of others, Seeing them both as having the nature of decay?
gm: Having gone to the charnel ground, The bones of others and my own body, As having the nature of perishing, When will I view them equally?

dm: This very body of mine Will eventually become such that Even jackals will not approach it Because of its stench.
gm: Even this very body of mine, By whose stench even foxes Will not approach near, Will become exactly like that.

dm: Although this body arose as a single entity, The flesh and bones that were born with it Will disintegrate and separate; What need is there to mention other loved ones?
gm: Although this body arose as one, The flesh and bones that were born together Will perish and separate from one another; What need to mention other friends?

dm: One is born alone, And likewise, one dies alone; Since others do not take a share of one's suffering, What use are friends who only create obstacles?
gm: When born, one is born alone, And when dying, one dies alone; Since no other takes a share of the suffering, What is the use of friends who are hindrances?

dm: Just as travelers on a road Take up a temporary lodging, So too do those on the path of existence Take up a place of birth.
gm: Just as those who enter upon a journey Take up a place to stay, In the same way, those entered on the path of existence Fully take up a place of birth.

dm: While the world is grieving all around, As long as this body has not yet Been carried away by four men, In the meantime, I shall go to the forest.
gm: While the whole world mourns, As long as four men Have not carried this away from there, Until then, go to the forest.

dm: Having made myself free of friends and free of enemies, This body shall dwell alone in a secluded place; Regarding myself as already dead, There will be no mourning even when I actually die.
gm: Having made no friends and no enemies, This body dwelling alone in solitude, Having considered it as already dead, Even when dying, there is no mourning.

dm: Since there is no one nearby To cause the harm of mourning, No one at all will distract me From such practices as the recollection of the Buddha.
gm: Since there is no one staying nearby To cause grief or harm, By this, the recollection of the Buddha and so forth Will not be distracted by anyone.

dm: Therefore, in a forest that is exceedingly delightful, Free of hardship, blissful, and the pacifier Of all distractions, I shall dwell entirely alone.
gm: Therefore, in exceptionally delightful Forests, with little trouble and happy, Pacifying all distractions, I shall dwell completely alone.
